#7785. If You Spot OTR on a Truck, Here’s What It Means

Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving. Learn what OTR means and how different trucking routes work.

Trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose. Some have long spikes on their wheels. Others might feature amber lights on top. You might even see diamond shaped signs. But what about OTR written on a truck?

What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry. Learn what OTR means, how long-haul work compares with shorter routes, and why the context matters.

In trucking, OTR stands for “over-the-road.” It refers to long-haul trucking, where drivers transport freight across long distances, often through several states or into Canada. According to trucking company Schneider, OTR drivers can spend weeks away from home. Many drive trucks with sleeper cabs that provide a place to rest between shifts.

OTR describes the type of work, not a specific truck. It’s also not a required marking. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires certain identifying information, including a company’s name and USDOT number, on interstate commercial trucks, but OTR isn’t part of that requirement.

The letters can also mean something different depending on where they appear. In the tire industry, OTR stands for “off-the-road,” referring to heavy-duty tires used on construction and mining equipment. OTR Diagnostics is also the name of a maintenance tool that helps truck owners check engine problems and other vehicle information.

OTR truck drivers transport freight over long distances, often making several stops along the way. Their jobs can also involve inspecting their trucks, handling delivery paperwork, and sometimes helping load or unload cargo.

Because these trips can last for weeks, drivers often sleep in their trucks or stop at other places along their routes. The FMCSA limits how long commercial drivers can drive without taking required breaks and rest periods.

Drivers who operate most full-size tractor-trailers need a Class A commercial driver’s license (CDL). Depending on the company and route, drivers may spend several weeks working before returning home.

OTR drivers cover the longest distances and may spend weeks away from home. Regional drivers work within a particular area of the country, often returning home weekly or more frequently. Local drivers generally stay closer to home and return after each shift, although they can still work long hours.

There’s also dedicated trucking, where drivers regularly transport freight for the same customer or between the same locations. These routes can be local, regional, or long-distance, depending on the company.

The exact distances and schedules vary between employers, so the terms don’t always describe the same mileage or amount of time away from home.

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:58 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

As November rolls around and people bring out their holiday décor, many choose to display candles to cultivate a warm, inviting atmosphere throughout the holiday season. Candles can brighten a room, shift the mood, provide soothing scents, and offer a pop of color. However, some homeowners shy away from using open-flame candles because they come with a fire safety hazard.

Battery-operated candles provide a great alternative to traditional candles that are aesthetically pleasing, says Kanika Bakshi Khurana, principal interior designer and founder of Kanika Design in San Mateo, California. “In addition to providing a less hazardous option for displaying during holidays, battery-operated candles provide a practical solution for those who may be too busy with other activities,” explains Khurana. Also, they don’t leave soot or wax on surfaces like traditional candles do, and you save money from not having to continually purchase replacement candles once they burn down completely. “The added feature of being able to control how long each candle is lit through timers and remote controls provides additional convenience in using these types of candles,” she adds.

Here are several battery-operated candle ideas for decorating your home this winter season.

Operated by an intelligent remote control, these realistic flameless candles use a new technology to simulatef real flickering candles.

Battery-operated candles can be used to safely illuminate items displayed on your fireplace mantel. Khurana recommends creating a layering of candles on the mantel by using multiple battery-operated candles of varying heights and combining them with assorted décor items, such as greenery, pine cones, or branches for an element of depth in the winter design. “When using flames that have a gentle flicker, you will find this candle arrangement to be more visually appealing, particularly when lit at night,” she says.

Bookshelves and built-in cabinets—and the items displayed on them like framed pictures and sculptures—are often stunning during the daylight hours but offer no visual interest when darkness falls. Khurana suggests placing small, battery-operated candles inside decorative glass vases or on open shelves with your books and ceramics. “The light will create a warm ambiance for the area and make the surrounding objects appear as if they are illuminated,” she explains. And with battery-operated candles, you won’t be stuck trying to get candle wax out of your vase or jar the next day.

Set up a safe, inviting environment for guests by displaying battery-operated candles instead of open-flame candles in windows and throughout your entryway. “An entryway can be one of the first areas in your home where you use battery-operated candles to set the tone for when people enter your house,” says Khurana. “It is easy to arrange two or three flameless candle pillars on a console table with some other objects, a small seasonal flower arrangement, and a decorative mirror, which will help reflect the light created by the candles and enhance the welcoming atmosphere.”

Flameless tapers and other types of candles are perfect for creating that warm, candlelight vibe at your holiday dinner table, while providing peace of mind for you and your family as they dine with you, says Khurana. “Place each taper into a vintage brass holder (mixing high and low) down the middle of your holiday dining table and add a simple arrangement of fresh greenery and/or seasonal fruits to create a stunning holiday centerpiece.”

Using battery operated candles, you can create a warm and cozy atmosphere in your bedroom without setting an actual candle near your bedding or curtains, notes Khurana. She suggests placing two of these small candles together on a dresser or beside a photo frame on a nightstand and adding a vase between them. “This will help you slowly shift from being awake during the day to being relaxed at night,” she says.

Flameless candles also look fabulous inside lanterns, which come in a wide variety of sizes, materials, and colors. “A couple ways I have used this idea is to place a large lantern next to a fireplace or to group two lanterns of varying sizes together at the base of an entryway console,” says Khurana. “To create a more elegant look for your lanterns, you can choose from antique brass, black metal, or natural wood options, and instead of using bright and cool-toned light bulbs, use warm white candle lights.” For out-of-reach spots, you can even choose remote-controlled flameless candles for easy operation.

#7783. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

#7782. 6 Tricks to Get Back Into Your House After Getting Locked Out

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 6, 2026 11:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Q: Last night I was almost locked out of the house, as I nearly left my keys on the counter before walking to a neighborhood BBQ. That got me thinking—what should I have done if I locked myself out of my house? And are there steps I can take to make sure it never happens? I’m thinking of giving a spare key to a neighbor, but I’m unsure what else can be done!

A: Getting locked out of your house can be a frustrating experience, but it’s not as uncommon as you may think. And unless you’re prepared, the situation can be more terrifying than it has to be.

Thankfully, there are plenty of ways to get back inside a house without breaking in through your door, even if all signs point to the opposite. From checking windows or removing door knobs to calling a locksmith or family member with a spare key, there’s no shortage of options at your disposal. Once you get back inside, you can then take steps to protect yourself from getting locked out again. This includes installing smart locks or hiding a key in a secure location somewhere else on your property.

If your door lock is locked and you’re outside the home, the first thing to do is stay calm. It’s easy to panic, but there are several ways to remedy the situation. Here’s a look at actions you can take to get back inside.

The quickest way to get back inside a home when locked out of the house with no key is by searching for another door or window that may be unlocked. Whether it’s a back door or basement window, be sure to check all entryways that are reasonably accessible. This might mean removing or damaging a window screen, but if it’s the difference between being locked outside and getting back inside, that’s a small price to pay. If there’s no easy way to get to the second-story windows, it’s best to leave them be—there are plenty of other ways to get inside, so there’s no reason to risk an injury.

If a family member, friend, or neighbor has a spare key, now is the time to try and contact them. People locked out of their homes who still have their smartphones with them can place a quick call to the owner of their spare. If the cell phone is inside the house, consider asking a neighbor or walking to a local shop and using their phone. This won’t be possible in all locations (especially in rural areas), but it’s a nice backup if a smartphone isn’t readily available. At any rate, contacting the person responsible for the spare key should be a top priority.

Individuals locked out of a rental unit can contact either their landlord or the maintenance company to help get back inside. The landlord will almost certainly have a spare key. If the rental unit is part of a large apartment building, there’s likely a maintenance technician on site who can help instead of the landlord. Many apartments also have a leasing office, so if someone is locked out of an apartment and doesn’t have the contact details for maintenance or their landlord, they can try this location as a backup. Most leasing offices are staffed during normal business hours and are more than willing to help tenants locked outside their apartments.

Though it’s not easy, attempting to pick the lock is worth consideration. Some door latches can be reached with a twisted paper clip or credit card. To attempt this, the card or paper clip needs to slip past the strike plate and catch the door latch. Once the latch is caught, it can be pushed out of place and the door can be opened. If the deadbolt is in place, this technique will not work. But if it’s just a simple latch on a door knob, it’s certainly worth a try. Unlocking a door this way is tricky, though it may be effective in some situations.

Another possible way to get back inside is to remove the door knob. This requires users to have access to a standard toolkit, though often just a screwdriver can get the job done. Most knobs don’t have exposed screws on their exterior plate, but it’s possible to gain access to them by looking for a small slot somewhere else on its faceplate. This small slot keeps the knob and faceplate in place—by depressing it, users can remove the faceplate and gain access to the screws.

With the screws exposed, they can be loosened and the door knob can be removed. This gives access to the lock’s inner workings, part of which includes a mechanism for opening the door. Try using a screwdriver to twist the inner component, which should unlock the latch. Keep in mind these general steps won’t work for all types of locks, as each model is unique. For detailed steps, it’s a good idea to look up installation instructions for the specific brand in question.

The simplest way to unlock a locked door is by contacting a locksmith. These trained professionals can not only circumvent a locked door, but they’re trained to also repair or replace the lock once the door is open. The process typically doesn’t take very long, with many home lockout services lasting no more than an hour.

Pricing for locksmiths varies by location, but in an emergency situation, they’re worth every penny. Many locksmiths deal with more than just residential homes, making them a great choice when locked out of a car, RV, or any other building. They can even rekey a lock and help people locked out with the key stuck in the door. They are also trained to assist with changing locks on the door if an upgrade or replacement is required. So if none of the above steps work, a locksmith offering house lockout service is the best option.

While accidents can happen to anyone, there are steps people can take to prevent future house lockouts. This includes simple things like hiding a spare key somewhere around the property and giving a spare to a neighbor, along with more complicated tasks like installing smart locks. Not all of these steps will apply to all homes, but the more failsafes in place, the better the odds of getting back inside.

Installing one of the best security systems (such as Vivint or ADT) is a great way to keep burglars at bay and improve home security. If the system also includes a smart lock, users have a quick way to get back inside when locked out. In fact, many smart locks are designed in a way that makes it nearly impossible to get locked out, as they can be controlled with a physical key or the built-in keypad.

With a traditional lock, leaving the key inside the home results in a lockout. With a smart lock, leaving the key inside simply means users need to use their digital code to get back inside. Some of the best smart locks, like the Yale Assure Lock 2, also work with mobile companion apps, letting users open the door with their smartphone.

Alternatively, many of the best electronic door locks toe the line between traditional and smart locks, making them a good choice for homes looking for the best of both worlds. It’s important to read up on what smart locks are before making a purchase, as well as learn about the types of door locks available, as there are advantages and disadvantages to them all.

While shopping for a security system and smart lock, homeowners can also pick up other security gear, including the best door security bars to help prevent break-ins.

Giving a key to a trusted neighbor or nearby family member is a simple (yet effective) way to prevent getting locked out. Ideally, this will be someone easy to reach and within walking distance of the home, ensuring they can quickly get to the home without requiring a phone call or a long drive.

However, it’s important to have complete trust in the person receiving the spare key. Not only can they help during lockouts, but they can essentially enter the home whenever they’d like. This makes it important to only pass out spare keys to neighbors who have proven themselves to be responsible and trustworthy. Otherwise, this step could result in more headaches than it’s worth.

Hiding a spare key on the property is another popular way to ensure lockouts never happen, but this needs to be handled with care. Ideally, a lock box with a spare key inside will be installed near the front door, allowing only people with the password access to the spare. This is leagues better than simply hiding a key under the doormat or inside a yard decoration, as anyone who stumbles upon the key will be able to get into the home.

If a lockbox isn’t used, then ensure that the hidden spare key is in a location that won’t be disturbed by harsh weather or easily seen by prying eyes. This includes inside a dog house, under a brick or patio paver, inside a magnetic holder placed under a bench, or stowed away inside a fake rock. Poor locations to hide a key include under a doormat, under a flowerpot, or on top of the door frame.

Keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse comes with serious drawbacks. For one, if the wallet or purse is lost, someone will now have a key to the home, meaning it’s best to have the lock rekeyed. If the key is placed in a purse or wallet without a way to keep it secure, it’s also possible for it to slip out while reaching for a credit card or cash. Because of this, anyone storing a key in their wallet or purse will need to invest in a key holder—these are cheap, secure, and prevent the key from rubbing against the wall of the wallet and piercing its side.

The benefits of keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse may outweigh the drawbacks, especially for people who never leave home without their purse or wallet. This essentially gives individuals another way to get back inside their home without requiring their keychain.

The simplest way to prevent a lockout is to get in the habit of never leaving home without a set of keys. This is easier said than done, but certain actions help turn this into a routine. Many people prefer to place a dish or tray near their front door for valuables like their keys. When leaving the home, having the keys right next to the exit makes it virtually impossible to forget them. Other people like to use a keychain that’s visually appealing, ensuring it catches their eyes when leaving the home.

Aside from making the keys easy to spot when leaving, good habits include reserving a specific pocket for keys, checking for keys before closing any lockable door, and communicating with family members or roommates to ensure they don’t get locked out if no one else is home.

Getting locked out of the house can be a frightening experience. Thankfully, there are several ways to remedy the situation and get back inside. From asking a neighbor for a spare and checking for unlocked windows to calling a locksmith or attempting to pick the lock, there’s an option that works for everyone.

The best option is to prevent lockouts from happening in the first place. To that end, installing smart locks and stashing a spare key on the property are both great options. Each home will have techniques that work better than others, and it’s up to each individual to determine what works best for them.

#7781. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7780. Impeach Pete Hegseth

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

He deserves it for his role in starting an unconstitutional war and perpetrating over 200 murders.

Outgoing GOP Representative Thomas Massie is planning to introduce an impeachment resolution against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Soon-to-be Democratic Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries says he's a "hard yes" on the idea. That makes it very likely it will happen. If not now, then when Democrats take control of Congress in January, after their big win in the midterm election. Hegseth richly deserves it, and should be convicted on at least two major charges: his role in starting an unconstitutional war and over 200 cases of outright murder.

On September 15, Rep. Massie outlined eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth (see here for his more detailed description). The two most compelling are these:

Article I - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 2(c): Charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat. It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception….

Article V - Extrajudicial Killings: Charges Secretary Hegseth with replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers, resulting in at least 221 deaths. It also addresses denial of quarter, secondary strikes on survivors, failure to rescue shipwrecked persons, and the creation of artificial legal authorities for the campaign.

Massie's Article V is the single most damning, in my view. Hegseth is a principal architect of the Trump Administration's campaign of "drug boat" strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific. It has now killed an estimated 244 people, virtually all of them civilians (Massie's September figure of 221 is now somewhat outdated).

I have previously written about why these strikes are illegal (see here and here). But don't take my word for it, or even that of other libertarian or left-liberal experts, like Brian Finucane. Take that of John Yoo, former Bush Administration official, and leading academic advocate of sweeping executive power over foreign policy and national security issues. If you illegally order the deliberate killing of civilians - especially outside the context of a war - that's outright murder. And that's exactly what Pete Hegseth has done.

This would be true even if those killed were all would-be drug dealers seeking to transport illegal drugs for sale in the US. I have previously explained why it is unjust and illegal to kill suspected drug dealers out of hand and why they are not the legal or moral equivalent of terrorists or enemy combatants in a war. As GOP Sen. Rand Paul pointed out when the drug boat strikes began, "The reason we have trials and we don't automatically assume guilt is what if we make a mistake and they happen to be people fleeing the Venezuelan dictator? … off our coast it isn't our policy just to blow people up … even the worst people in our country, they still get a trial." But, in fact, the evidence indicates most were not on their way to the US and many were not transporting drugs at all. Some, for example, were just fishermen.

The Constitution allows impeachment and removal of executive branch officials for "high crimes and misdemeanors." You don't have to be a lawyer or legal scholar to figure out that complicity in over 200 murders qualifies as a "high crime."

Hegseth is also a key architect of the disastrous Iran War. In previous writings, I have explained why that war is illegal, violating both the Constitution, and the War Powers Act of 1973. Such a war requires congressional authorization, and Trump and Hegseth did not even try to get it. The war's illegality is one of the main reasons for its failure to this point, as failure to secure the broad public support needed to get congressional authorization  ensured Trump lacked staying power to continue the fight effectively after the initial strikes didn't achieve a quick, decisive victory.

Initiating and waging an illegal war isn't a violation of criminal law (though perhaps it should be). But massive non-criminal illegal acts and abuses of power are impeachable under the history and original meaning of the Impeachment Clause of the Constitution. On that point, see analyses by Gene Healy of the Reason Foundation (formerly at the Cato Institute), and prominent conservative legal scholars Michael Stokes Paulsen (here, here, and here), and Keith Whittington. There are few bigger illegal abuses of power than starting a massive unconstitutional war.

In fairness, Trump and Hegseth are not alone in starting illegal wars. Barack Obama did it, too, with his unconstitutional wars against Libya and ISIS (which, for those keeping score, I condemned at the time). Obama likely deserved to be impeached, as well. But the fact that he got away with this illegality is no reason to spare Hegseth. To the contrary, past laxness is all the more reason to reestablish deterrence to prevent future wrongdoing. Furthermore, Trump and Hegseth's illegal war is on a much larger scale than Obama's were, and has had far worse results.

The only potentially valid objection to impeaching Hegseth is that it might fail, and backfire politically. But the Iran War is highly unpopular, and therefore impeachment on that basis is unlikely to backfire. The politics of the boat strikes is more debatable. The administration will surely try to defend them by arguing the victims deserved it because they were trying to smuggle dangerous drugs. But that can be countered by presenting the extensive evidence demonstrating that many were not on their way to the US or even transporting drugs at all. Testimony from members of the bereaved families of the victims can help make that point, and influence public opinion against Hegseth and the administration.

Hegseth is unpopular on Capitol Hill, which makes it potentially possible to secure the needed 11 or more GOP senators' votes required for conviction (the Democrats are going to have 54-56 senators in the next Congress, depending on the results of still-ongoing vote counts in close races in Alaska and Mississippi). But even if he gets acquitted, the process of impeachment and trial can send a useful signal, and further publicize the administration's massive criminality and wrongdoing.

Obviously, the ultimate perpetrator of these illegal acts is not Hegseth, but Trump. The former was following the latter's illegal orders (though he likely also helped influence Trump to give those orders in the first place). But sanctioning officials for obeying illegal orders is still important. That's one of the lessons of the Nuremberg trials. And, hopefully, the time will come for Trump to face sanctions for his many illegal actions, as well. As with Hegseth, the only plausible argument against impeaching him is political, not legal or moral.

Massie's impeachment resolution also outlines several other charges against Hegseth. I think most of them have merit, but are less significant than those covered above. I will not attempt to assess these other charges here.

UPDATE: Back in 2020, I critiqued the "slippery slope" argument against impeaching presidents for abuses of power that aren't technically crimes. My points apply with even greater force to any such argument against impeaching appointed officials, like Hegseth. In their case, there is no argument they have some kind of popular mandate from the electorate.

#7778. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

#7777. Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

“Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”

“This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

#7774. Second Amendment Roundup: Viramontes Is Not Moot

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Cook County includes AK-47 rifles to be among “AR-15 platform weapons”

In the Viramontes v. Cook County case pending in the Supreme Court, Cook County has filed a Suggestion of Mootness in response to a Motion to Dismiss Petitioner Cutberto Viramontes from the case.  The question presented in the case is: "Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles."  Cook County argues that standing in the challenge is based on Mr. Viramontes' wish to obtain an AR-15 style rifle, but Christopher Khaya, the only other individual petitioner in the case, only wishes to obtain an AK-47 style rifle.  Mr. Khaya, the argument goes, does not have standing to litigate the question presented because he did not state he wishes to obtain an AR-15.

Yet Cook County itself previously classified the AK-47 as within the general category "AR-15 platform weapons."  The Brief for the Cook County Respondents states:

Specific firearms are outlawed under the Ordinance, including the "AK-47," "AR-15," "Bushmaster XM15," "Bushmaster Carbon 15," "Bushmaster MOE series," "ArmaLite M15," "Armalite M15-T," and "Olympic Arms PCR." [Cook County, Ill., Code of Ordinances] § 54-211(7) (hereafter AR-15 platform weapons).

The County uses the term "AR-15 platform weapons" throughout its Brief as a convenient shorthand to describe the types of rifles it bans.  For instance, referring to how "the public increasingly purchased AR-15 platform weapons," in the next sentence it describes a shooting in which the perpetrator used "a semiautomatic AK-47 style rifle."  Describing the features that tie such rifles together, the Brief states: "The Ordinance is limited to 'assault weapons' that are strictly defined as 'semiautomatic rifle[s]' able to accept a detachable large capacity magazine and one or more of certain military-style features, such as a folding or telescoping stock, a pistol grip without a stock, a barrel shroud, or a muzzle brake."  (There is actually nothing specifically "military-style" about such features.)

In its Suggestion of Mootness, the County attempts to separate these common features by distinguishing the different model names and designs.  Viramontes sought "to own a Smith and Wesson Military & Police AR-15 style semiautomatic rifle," while Khaya "wants an IMI [Industrial Military Industries] Galil semiautomatic rifle," which the petitioners themselves stated "is not an AR-15 style rifle but is largely based on the AK-47 design."  But the question presented is not that narrow, instead referring generally to "AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles."  To that, the County claims: "There are no record facts concerning whether the IMI Galil weapon operates similarly to an AR-15."  For starters, how about the County's own Brief describing their common features to be that they are semiautomatic rifles, have the ability to accept a detachable magazine, and have a pistol grip, folding or telescoping stock, and a muzzle brake?

In sum, in its Brief, Cook County refers to "AK-47" rifles as encompassed in the general term "AR-15 platform weapons."  Its denial of that in its Suggestion of Mootness cannot be regarded as well taken.  Mr. Khaya has standing to litigate the question presented.  There are also two association challengers who thereby also have standing.

In any event, as Cook County notes in its filing, Viramontes is consolidated with Grant v. Higgins, the challenge to Connecticut's prohibition on semiautomatic rifles, which is quite similar to that of Cook County. Therefore, regardless of what happens with Cook County's suggestion of mootness, the Grant case will be unaffected, and the Supreme Court is poised to decide this fundamental issue that lays at the heart of the Second Amendment.

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

#7773. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7772. Wolverine Loader II Review: No Break-In, No Blisters

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

New work boots can be miserable until they’re broken in, especially if you spend long days on your feet. My husband, a contractor who also works on our farm, tested the Wolverine Loader II HyperRest CarbonMAX boots for a full week, wearing them up to 10 hours a day. We had previously tested two of Wolverine’s Infinity System work boots, so we were curious to compare them with this pair’s comfort design. Here’s what we found. (And for more options, see our team-tested best work boots guide.)

The break-in was the biggest surprise of our test. My husband put the Wolverine Loader II boots on and went straight to work. There was no period of stiff leather rubbing against his ankles, no uncomfortable pressure around his toes, and no need to alternate with an older pair while the new boots softened up.

He wore them for a week while doing his regular contracting work and handling chores on our farm, including clearing trees and operating equipment. Some days stretched to 10 hours, but he never complained about sore feet afterward.

Wolverine credits much of that comfort to its (removable) HyperRest footbed, which cushions and supports the foot, and a polyurethane midsole that helps absorb the impact of walking on hard surfaces. The padded collar also helps prevent rubbing around the ankle. Whatever the combination, it worked well for him from the first day.

In our testing, yes. My husband is accustomed to wearing work boots, so he knows the difference between a pair that feels good in the store and one that remains comfortable through a full shift.

The Loader II passed that test. He especially liked how light they felt for boots with protective toes. Wolverine lists the weight at 2.04 pounds per boot, and the CarbonMAX composite toe provides impact and compression protection without the bulk of a traditional steel toe.

The rubber wedge outsole is another feature of the comfort design. Its broad contact area helps distribute weight on hard, flat surfaces, which can be particularly helpful for contractors who spend hours on concrete or other unforgiving flooring.

The Wolverine Loader II is more than just a comfortable boot. Its CarbonMAX toe meets ASTM F2413-24 impact and compression requirements, and the boot also carries electrical hazard and slip-resistance ratings.

The waterproof full-grain leather upper includes reinforced toe and heel bumpers, which help protect areas that often take a beating around tools, equipment, and construction materials. A breathable waterproof membrane and moisture-wicking lining provide additional protection in wet conditions.

Wolverine also uses Goodyear welt construction, which allows the boots to be resoled rather than discarded when the outsole wears out. That’s a welcome feature in a work boot intended for regular use.

One consideration is the wedge outsole. While it’s designed for dependable traction, its relatively flat profile didn’t dig into deep mud as aggressively as some heavily lugged soles. For workers who spend most of their time in muddy fields or on steep, loose terrain, outsole design deserves extra attention.

At $169.95, the Loader II is cheaper than the premium Wolverine Infinity System boots we previously tested, yet it delivered the comfort my husband needs for long workdays.

I think these boots are particularly well suited to contractors, carpenters, equipment operators, and other tradespeople who want safety-toe protection without stiff, heavy footwear. The 6-inch lace-up design also provides a more adjustable fit than a pull-on boot.

After a week of demanding use, my husband had no complaints about comfort, fit, or foot fatigue. That’s an excellent start, although we’ll need more time to judge how the leather, stitching, and outsole hold up over months of daily wear.

For workers who dread breaking in a new pair of boots, the Loader II might just be the ticket.

#7771. 16 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds’ slats, however, are usually an inch wide or narrower. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Because vinyl blinds are made from PVC and other synthetic materials, they’re a great choice for bathrooms, kitchens, and other areas prone to moisture and humidity. They’re very easy to clean with a cloth or a vacuum attachment. If you’re looking for a window treatment that helps insulate your windows or provides soundproofing, vinyl isn’t your best bet. Still, they are a lot cheaper than wood and other options, if you’re on a budget.

Best For: Budget-conscious shoppers; moisture-prone rooms

Ideal for high-humidity spaces like garages and bathrooms, Bali’s 2-inch vinyl blinds resist chipping and warping and come in dozens of colors.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Sometimes you want the timeless look of a wood blind but don’t have the budget for it. Enter the faux wood blind, which is usually made from PVC or a wood/synthetic blend. Faux wood blinds look like the real deal (though your mileage may vary when it comes to how authentic the wood grain looks), at a fraction of the price. The best part? They can be installed in high-humidity spaces like laundry rooms and bathrooms, where natural wood blinds would mold and warp.

Best for: Budget-conscious homeowners who want a timeless look

Blinds.com’s faux wood blinds are moisture resistant, and available in a variety of wood stains and painted colors.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are modern window coverings that you can open and close using a remote control, phone app, or via voice command. Some models have light sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that are adjusted manually, motorized blinds have electric or battery-powered motors that raise and lower them. If you want to be able to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat, opt for blinds with this feature.

Custom Home Collection’s wood blinds come in over 100 colors and a motorized lift option, which is ideal for smart homes and hard-to-reach windows.

Coolaroo’s knitted HDPE roller shades are mold resistant and block 90 percent of UV rays. Read the review.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Chicology’s zebra blinds are cordless (and thus kid-friendly), light-filtering, and come in three colors.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy efficiency; homes with a modern vibe

Noise-dampening, cordless, and energy-efficient, the BlindsAvenue honeycomb blinds can be mounted inside or outside the window.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist look.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

These cordless, pull-down blackout blinds from Persilux are available in five colors and multiple sizes.

#7769. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.
